My wife and I both have top tier (above 800) credit. Our only loan is on a house, and in reality we could empty our savings (not retirement, savings) and pay it off... but to what benefit? Completely eradicating our emergency fund? To remove a $300 monthly bill? Depending on what the market is like when we hit 50% equity, we may refinance and take some cash out to further our investment portfolio... cheapest loan anyone is ever likely to get.

But I've also seen cash-only people (my brother-in-law) struggle and get raked over the coals because of no credit. He wanted to buy a home and had to have his folks co-sign, as a 30y/o man with a good job and no debt. And I know others with 6-figure salaries who have reasonably good credit but are one month away from disaster, can't afford to furnish their McMansions and sometimes go hungry. All in the name of image.

That doesn't mean that playing the game for credit scores is good or bad, it's just a game. It's inevitable in the current version of society. Basically breaks down to how much value your "word" has, if you say you're going to pay for something, will you actually pay for it? Integrity of sorts... it's flawed and can easily be gamed, but there is absolutely no downside to having a good credit score. None. When something has zero negative, all positive and can be gotten with Less effort than you spend by avoiding the game, it just sorta sets you off to the side in a coral labeled "oddity".

And yes, credit unions are FAR superior to "banks". The longer you have an account with them the more weight your requests hold too... I had an account with one starting when I was 13, went to buy a house when I was 31 and they blew away the competition for home loans. If you go that route, the next time you want to buy a new motorcycle, ask them for a secured loan. You give the bank the sum you want to borrow, they invest it and you make "payments". Huge bonus to your credit score, but you can cash out pretty much any time (last one I had there was a penalty for early payment within the first year).
